title: xView2 machine-learning damage maps may have been used by UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, the World Bank, IFRC and WFP after the 6 February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes
summary: MIT Technology Review (20 February 2023), quoting DIU: xView2 used by two UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP; Microsoft reports 3,849 damaged buildings mapped for AFAD.
account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives February 9, 2023, as the first usable-image date. However, the linked technical report includes February 7 imagery for Islahiye and February 9 imagery for the other three cities. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from February 7 to February 9. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.
purpose: Rapid building-damage assessment from pre- and post-event satellite imagery for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. This use was that purpose.
system: xView2 building damage assessment models (semantic segmentation on satellite imagery, trained on the xBD dataset)
developer: US Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) with Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute; research partners Microsoft AI for Good and UC Berkeley
deployer: UN INSARAG (search and rescue ground teams in Adıyaman); AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP (per the developer's account); Microsoft AI for Good delivered estimates to AFAD (per Microsoft)
location: Adıyaman and four cities in southeast Türkiye including Kahramanmaraş (Marash)

fields.account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives February 9, 2023, as the first usable-image date. However, the linked technical report includes February 7 imagery for Islahiye and February 9 imagery for the other three cities. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from February 7 to February 9. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

fields.account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives February 9, 2023, as the first usable-image date. However, the linked technical report includes February 7 imagery for Islahiye and February 9 imagery for the other three cities. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from February 7 to February 9. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.
